explanations.explanation: Chronicles says it flat out: Reuben's "birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel" (1 Chronicles 5:1). Reuben was first in line and still got passed over. Friend, that's like being first to the cookie table and finding the plate already empty. And he is not reckoned according to birthright.

I see why you'd say Judah. Judah, another son of Israel (Genesis 35:23), is the one who prevailed over his brothers, and a ruler came from him. But the very next verse says "the birthright belonged to Joseph" (1 Chronicles 5:2). Judah got the ruler, Joseph got the birthright. Two different prizes.

Levi, another son of Israel (Genesis 35:23), never shows up in this part of the story. The names Chronicles gives are Joseph and Judah. The text says the birthright "was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel" (1 Chronicles 5:1). Levi's name isn't on this one, friend.

Yes, friend! "A ruler came from him," says Chronicles about Judah (1 Chronicles 5:2). Judah prevailed over his brothers. And still the birthright belonged to Joseph. That's two different blessings going to two different brothers.

Good guess, but priest isn't the word in this verse. Chronicles says Judah prevailed over his brothers and "a ruler came from him" (1 Chronicles 5:2). So the blank is ruler. Meanwhile the birthright stays with Joseph, so keep those two prizes apart.

Prophet is a fine word, but this verse doesn't use it. What it says is that Judah prevailed over his brothers and "a ruler came from him" (1 Chronicles 5:2). So the blank is ruler, not prophet. The birthright stays with Joseph the whole time.

Livestock it is, friend! "Their livestock had increased in the land of Gilead," and that's why the Reubenites settled so far east (1 Chronicles 5:9). More animals means more room needed. It's like a closet that's full and you keep buying more stuff anyway.

Enemies do show up in this passage, with the Hagrites coming in the next verse. But the reason Chronicles gives for spreading east is different. It says "their livestock had increased in the land of Gilead" (1 Chronicles 5:9). So the blank is livestock.

Chronicles doesn't mention troubles here, friend. The text gives a plain reason for the Reubenites spreading east: "their livestock had increased in the land of Gilead" (1 Chronicles 5:9). More animals, more land needed. The blank is livestock.

It's the other way around, friend. In the days of Saul, king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), the Reubenites "waged war against the Hagrites, who were defeated at their hands" (1 Chronicles 5:10). So the Hagrites lost, not the Reubenites. After that, the Reubenites occupied the Hagrites' dwellings east of Gilead.

False is right! The text says the Hagrites "were defeated at their hands" (1 Chronicles 5:10). The Reubenites won that war. Then they moved into the Hagrites' dwellings throughout the region east of Gilead. That's a good day for them, friend.

That's the one. "Because they cried out to God in battle, they were helped against their enemies" (1 Chronicles 5:20). Right in the middle of the fight, they cried out to God. I'd say that's the best move you can make with 44,760 warriors standing right there.

explanations.answer: They call to Judah for help
explanations.explanation: Chronicles never says they called on Judah. It tells us what they did in battle: "they cried out to God" (1 Chronicles 5:20). And that's why they were helped against their enemies. The text points up, friend, not sideways.

More soldiers might seem like a smart move, but that's not what the verse says. They already had 44,760 warriors trained for battle (1 Chronicles 5:18). What Chronicles tells us is that "they cried out to God in battle" (1 Chronicles 5:20). That's what comes before the help.

explanations.answer: They put their trust in Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Chronicles says it plainly: "Because they put their trust in God, He answered their prayers" (1 Chronicles 5:20). The reason is right there in the verse. They cried out, and they trusted Him.

Chronicles doesn't mention offerings here. It gives one reason: "Because they put their trust in God, He answered their prayers" (1 Chronicles 5:20). So the answer is trust, not a pile of gifts. Even a big box of cookies can't beat that.

explanations.answer: They had fought for Him before
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about past fights counting here. It says, "Because they put their trust in God, He answered their prayers" (1 Chronicles 5:20). The reason is trust, not their record. I think that's a kind way for it to work, baker.

That's right. "Many others fell slain, because the battle belonged to God" (1 Chronicles 5:22). This was God's battle from the start. That fits with what we just saw, that they cried out to Him and trusted Him.
Saul, king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), was reigning when this war happened. But the verse doesn't hand him the battle. It says "the battle belonged to God" (1 Chronicles 5:22). So the blank is God.
The Reubenites were fighting, sure. But the text doesn't say the battle was theirs. It says "the battle belonged to God" (1 Chronicles 5:22). So the blank is God, friend.

Yes. The heads of Manasseh's families were "mighty men of valor, famous men," and then comes the turn: "But they were unfaithful to the God of their fathers" (1 Chronicles 5:24-25). All that fame, and the story moves to unfaithfulness. I think this is a heavy part, baker, and it's worth a quiet pause.

Chronicles doesn't say the tribes fought each other. In fact, Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh fought the Hagrites together. What went wrong is this: "they were unfaithful to the God of their fathers" (1 Chronicles 5:25). That's the turn in the story.

No treaty with Egypt shows up in this passage, friend. Chronicles says it directly: "they were unfaithful to the God of their fathers" (1 Chronicles 5:25). That's what went wrong for these famous family heads. It's a sober verse.

True. The verse says they turned to "the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them" (1 Chronicles 5:25). So those were peoples God had already destroyed before them. It's a serious detail, baker, and the text states it plainly.

The verse says the opposite of False. They turned to "the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them" (1 Chronicles 5:25). So God had destroyed those peoples before them. The statement on the card matches the text.

That's right. "So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" to take them into exile (1 Chronicles 5:26). Pul is also called Tiglath-pileser. That verse comes right after the unfaithfulness in verse 25. It's a sober ending to a passage that started with a birthright.

The king of Judah isn't in this verse, friend. Chronicles says, "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" (1 Chronicles 5:26). So it's God of Israel who is named, not a king of Judah. It's a heavy verse, so I'm keeping my jokes in the oven.

Egypt doesn't appear in this verse. The text says "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" (1 Chronicles 5:26). Pul is also called Tiglath-pileser. So the answer is the God of Israel, friend.
